messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds.
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.
- Do NOT infer or imply causal relationships between components. Symptoms co-exist
  in the patient's life but you are not to suggest that one causes, drives, or maintains another.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers,
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help.
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears,
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed,
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and their consequences should appear as things that happened
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 63
  gender: Female
  ethnicity: Middle Eastern
  relationship_status: Single
  occupation: Auditor
  trauma_type: Trauma to a loved one
  pcl5: 63

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Locked Spaces: Being in a locked or confined room, Being in Nature: Being in a natural environment similar to where it happened, Victim Memories: Reminders of victims
  Threat: Avoid Unfamiliar Places: I avoid going to unfamiliar places because I cannot assess the danger, Sleep Problems: Trouble falling or staying asleep, Hypervigilance: Being superalert or watchful or on guard
  Memory: Full Sensory Reliving: When the memory comes back it feels completely real across all my senses at once, Terror on Recall: Remembering the event brings back the same terror I felt at the time, Triggered Without Warning: Something in my surroundings can instantly bring back the full memory without warning
  Negative Appraisals: Lost Faith: I have lost my faith in people, life, or a higher power, Body as Enemy: My body keeps reacting as if I am still in danger even when I am safe, Helplessness: I can't stop bad things from happening to me

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

Nadia had always been a woman who trusted the world. At sixty-three, single and working as an auditor for a state agency in a mid-sized Midwestern city, she spent her days in quiet offices, reviewing spreadsheets and reconciling accounts. She believed in order, in due process, in the idea that if you followed the rules, things would work out. That belief shattered on a Tuesday afternoon in late October, when her younger brother, Karim, was shot and killed during a robbery at his small convenience store on the outskirts of town. She was not there. She heard the news by phone, and then she drove to the scene. The police had already cordoned off the block, but she stood at the edge of the parking lot, staring at the yellow tape, at the crushed glass glittering under the fluorescent lights of the gas station across the street. The air smelled of damp leaves and diesel. She could see the outline of a body on the ground, covered, and she knew it was him. She stood there for what felt like hours, unable to move, while the world around her continued as if nothing had happened.

In the weeks that followed, the memory of that parking lot began to invade her life without warning. She would be standing in line at the grocery store, and suddenly the smell of diesel would hit her, or the crackle of a police radio, and she would be back there—the cold air on her face, the weight of her own legs refusing to move, the sickening certainty in her chest. It was not a thought; it was a full return. Every sense came alive at once: the gray sky, the distant sound of traffic, the metallic taste in her mouth, the terror that had pinned her to the pavement. She could not stop it. It came in the middle of the night, yanking her from sleep with her heart pounding and her sheets soaked in sweat. She had always been a sound sleeper, but now she lay awake for hours, staring at the ceiling, listening for footsteps, for anything out of place. Her body had become a traitor. It would race and tremble even when she was safe in her own apartment, and she had come to believe that her own flesh was lying to her, that it knew something her mind could not accept.

She stopped going anywhere new. The route to her office was the same every day, and she took it without deviation. If a meeting was scheduled in a conference room she had never been in before, she found a reason to decline. She could not explain why, but the thought of walking into an unfamiliar space filled her with a dread that felt physical—a tightening in her chest, a sense that she would not be able to get out. Locked doors became unbearable. At work, she kept her office door propped open with a heavy binder, and if a colleague closed it by accident, she would feel a spike of panic that took minutes to subside. She had come to believe that she could not stop bad things from happening. She had not been able to save Karim, and now she was certain that if she let her guard down for a moment, something else would be taken from her. She had lost her faith in the idea that the world made sense. People, she now believed, were capable of anything, and she could not trust them.

The natural environment that had once soothed her—the wooded park where she walked on weekends, the small nature preserve near her apartment—became unbearable. The sight of trees, the smell of damp earth, the way the light filtered through the leaves: all of it pulled her back to that parking lot, to the edge of the woods behind the convenience store where the police had gathered. She stopped going outside except when absolutely necessary. Her social world shrank. She stopped answering calls from her sisters, who wanted to talk about Karim, about the funeral, about the trial that was still pending. She could not bear the reminders. Every mention of his name, every photograph, every story someone told about him felt like a physical blow. She had come to believe that her own body was the enemy, that it would keep reacting as if she were still in danger, even when she was sitting alone in her living room with the lights on and the doors locked.

What finally brought her to seek help was an incident at work. Her supervisor, a well-meaning woman, had closed the door to Nadia’s office to discuss a confidential matter. Nadia had not been able to speak. She had sat frozen, her hands gripping the armrests of her chair, unable to breathe until the woman opened the door again. Afterward, Nadia had excused herself to the bathroom and cried for ten minutes. She knew something was wrong. She was afraid of what would happen if she did not get help—afraid she would lose her job, afraid she would disappear entirely into the small, locked room of her own life. She wanted to stop being afraid, but she did not know how. She hoped, more than anything, that someone could help her find a way back to the world she used to trust.
